before: So early on, the practice is finding out who's actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. You might catch yourself explaining who everybody is anyway. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody's around to take your cues from.
after: (then the next h2, Untangling the Belonging Bargains: identity formation also means untangling from family emotional systems, religious orthodoxies, group identities, political tribes and relationships that pull you away from your own knowing in exchange for belonging. The guide's last paragraph of this h2, that reparenting and identity-building can usually go on together and that making it safe is the first phase for some, is already in this h2's P2.)
guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Focusing can be especially useful for noticing feelings and preferences the conditioned self learned to overlook; you can then put tentative words to them, examine what they seem to mean, and revise your interpretation. Some people also benefit from temporary, intentional distance long enough for the conditioning to quiet down and authentic preferences to surface.

brief:
- Focusing can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the self you've been playing learned to overlook. Say in a few words what it is, since the reader hasn't met the term: Eugene Gendlin's method of paying attention to a vague, felt sense in your body until words come for it.
- then you can put tentative words to them, look at what they seem to mean, and revise how you read them (keep both "tentative" and "revise", or what surfaces becomes a verdict)
- some people also benefit from temporary, intentional distance, long enough for the conditioning to quiet down and real preferences to surface (an option for some people, not advice to step back from family or church)
- context, not for the text: the paragraph before ends on "what you believe and feel when nobody's around to take your cues from", and the one before that on the reader's guess ("lonely, probably?").
